sections.heading: Where a Bakersfield owner's week goes

blocks.text: The trades, the clinics, the ag suppliers, and the one person operations that make up most of Kern County share one problem: the person who does the work is also the person who answers the phone. A roofer in July cannot pick up. A front desk cannot text every no show. A consultant driving from Wasco to Arvin cannot type up the customer they just met. So the call goes to voicemail, the quote sits, and the admin waits until after dinner.
Every one of those is a repeatable task with a screen in it, which means software can do it. That is what an AI automation agency does, and it is most of what we do here.

blocks.text: Type "plumber" into Google from your phone and you get two things: the map pack with three businesses, and the regular results underneath. They are ranked by different systems.

blocks.title: The map pack
blocks.text: Your Google Business Profile: its category, its reviews, its distance from the searcher.

blocks.title: The regular results
blocks.text: Your website: a page for that service in that city, and the links pointing at it.

Winning one does not win the other, which is why so many local SEO services post to your profile every week and never move anything. We work both, in the order that matters. Our guide to [ranking higher on Google Maps](/blog/how-to-rank-higher-on-google-maps-a-comprehensive-guide) explains the map side in full if you want the long version first.

sections.heading: What ranks a Google Business Profile

blocks.text: The factors are measured every year by [Whitespark's Local Search Ranking Factors](https://whitespark.ca/local-search-ranking-factors/) survey, and the 2026 edition is blunt. The primary category is factor one of 187. Reviews, their recency, and a steady flow of them are the fastest rising signals. Keywords in the services field jumped from factor 110 to 35 in a single year. Google posts sit at 148.

So that is our order. Primary category read off the top three competitors in your market, not guessed. Every predefined service Google offers for your category, plus custom ones under the names customers search. Then a review process that runs every week: a direct link sent after the job, no gating, no incentives, and a reply from you within 48 hours. Then hours, attributes, description, and 8 to 12 photos of your work, because Google's Ask Maps answers questions straight from those fields now that Q&A is gone. The field by field detail is in our [Google Business Profile guide](/blog/google-business-profile-optimization-guide-2026).

We do not geotag photos, because Google strips the location data on upload and there is nothing left for it to affect. We do not stuff the business name with keywords, because that is the top cause of suspensions. And we do not post for the sake of posting.

sections.heading: What ranks your website locally

blocks.text: A dedicated page for each service you sell, written for your city, is the number one local organic factor. One page, about that service in that city, with your work on it, the reviews from there, and the answer to the searcher's question at the top.

We build those pages, wire them into your profile, and link them from the pages on your site that already get traffic. sections.heading: Storefronts, service areas, and several towns

blocks.title: Storefront or service area
blocks.text: A storefront shows its address and ranks around it. A service area business, the plumber or landscaper who works from home, hides the address and lists the towns it serves, and it ranks strongest near home. Both are legitimate; pretending to be the other one is the second most common reason a profile gets suspended.

blocks.title: Several towns

We start with the smaller towns nobody else is targeting, one page per town, each with something specific about that place and your work there. A landscaper serving five towns gets five pages over five weeks, not fifty in a weekend, because Google reads a batch of near identical pages as a doorway scheme and buries the whole domain.

blocks.text: Citations are your name, phone, and address on the directories that matter: Google, Apple, Bing, Facebook, Yelp, then the industry ones for your trade. sections.heading: What programmatic SEO is

blocks.text: A template, a dataset, and a rule that turns each row into a page. A lender publishes a page per city with live rate data. A software company publishes a page per integration. A directory publishes a page per product and location.

The pages rank because each one answers a search nobody has bothered to answer on its own, and there are hundreds of those searches. That is the promise, and it is real. Zillow, TripAdvisor, and NerdWallet are programmatic sites at heart.

sections.heading: When it works, and when it is spam

blocks.title: Google's own definition
blocks.text: Google's [spam policies](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies) name the failure mode directly. Scaled content abuse is "many pages generated for the primary purpose of manipulating search rankings and not helping users." Doorway abuse is pages "created to rank for specific, similar search queries" that lead to a weaker destination. A city page with the name swapped and nothing else changed is both.

blocks.title: Our test for every page
blocks.text: Does this page carry something no other page on the internet has? Your own numbers, your own inventory, your own measurements, a calculator, a comparison built from live data. If the answer is yes, the set can be large. If the answer is a paragraph of generic text and a different city in the H1, the set does not get built, and the call is where that gets decided, with your data on the screen.

sections.heading: How we build a page set

blocks.title: Research first
blocks.text: We pull search volume for the combinations you think people search, and we read the live results for a sample of them, because half the time the intent is not what the keyword tool says.

blocks.title: The data model
blocks.text: The page set is a product fed by a database, not a batch of articles, so we design the data model before the template. Where the data has to be pulled from somewhere, that is a [custom build](/services/custom-builds), and the pipeline gets written first.

blocks.title: A small first batch
blocks.text: The first batch is a test, not a launch. We ran that test on ourselves. In March 2026 we published 12 industry pages on our own site, one per keyword cluster, linked from the industries grid on our [services page](/services), and gated the second batch on Google indexing the first. Five months later only 2 of the 12 had earned a single impression in Search Console. So the second batch never got built, and those pages are being rewritten one at a time with data each page can call its own. That is the gate working. "Crawled, currently not indexed" is Google telling you the pages are thin, and publishing more of them makes it worse.

blocks.title: Internal links, then the next batch
blocks.text: Links from the pages that already get traffic, because an orphaned page set dies quietly no matter how good the template is. Only then does the next batch go out.

sections.heading: What we refuse to build

blocks.text: A services times cities matrix. Pages for towns you do not serve. A template that ships with a city name and nothing local underneath it. 300 pages in a week on a domain that has never published 30. Each of these has cost someone their rankings, and the June 2026 spam update was unusually fast about it.
If your customers are in one or two cities, you do not need programmatic SEO. You need a page per service, and that is [local SEO](/services/seo/local).

faqs.a: Publishing a set of pages from one template and one dataset, so that each search variation gets its own page without writing each one by hand. It works when every page holds data that differs from the others and is useful on its own. It fails when the pages are the same text with one word swapped.

sections.heading: What a website redesign changes

blocks.text: New copy that says what you do now. A layout built around one clear next step. Pages that load fast on a phone. A page for every service you sell, so each one can rank on its own. Forms that go to your inbox or your [CRM](/services/crm) instead of a dead mailbox.

blocks.text: The structure underneath: clean titles, one heading hierarchy, schema markup, and plain question and answer sections that AI assistants can quote.

blocks.title: What stays
blocks.text: The URLs that rank, the sentences that rank, and the reviews and photos that are yours. A redesign replaces what fails and keeps what works, which is why the audit comes before the design.

sections.heading: What we check before we quote

blocks.text: Most website redesign services start with a mood board. We start with Search Console. Before the proposal we run the current site through it and pull three lists. Every URL that has earned impressions in the last 16 months. Every URL with links from other sites pointing at it. Every page that is broken, duplicated, or thin. Then the mechanical checks: mobile rendering, load speed on a throttled connection, missing titles, headings that skip levels, forms that go nowhere. The third source is analytics: which pages get visited, where visitors leave, and which forms ever get filled in. A contact page nobody reaches is a navigation problem, not a copy problem, and the audit tells the two apart.

Those lists decide the shape of the project. A site with 40 pages and 6 that matter is a different job from a site with 40 pages that all rank for something. You see the lists on the call, so the quote makes sense to you.

sections.heading: What a redesign must not break

blocks.text: This is the part most redesigns get wrong, and it is why "we redesigned the site and traffic fell off a cliff" is such a common story.

An old site has history. Some of its pages rank, some have links from other sites, and some get impressions you never noticed. A redesign that changes every URL throws that history away. Google treats the new site as a stranger.

So the URLs that earn attention either stay exactly the same or get a single hop redirect to their replacement. No chains, no 404s on pages that rank, no changed headings on a page sitting at position two. Google publishes its own rules for [site moves with URL changes](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/site-move-with-url-changes), and we follow them.
If a page already ranks in the top three, we leave its content alone and redesign around it. You cannot beat first place by editing first place.

The first screen answers the four questions a visitor arrives with: what, for whom, where, and what happens next. Every service on its own page with a plain answer at the top. Only then does the design start, because the layout has to carry the message.
If your old copy has sentences that rank, they survive the rewrite. The audit tells us which ones.

sections.heading: Two kinds of website projects

blocks.title: No website yet
blocks.text: Some owners come to us with no website at all. A Facebook page, a Google listing, maybe a logo a cousin made. Customers find them anyway, then go quiet because there is nowhere to check what the business does.

blocks.title: A site from 2018
blocks.text: Others have a site that has not been touched since 2018. It loads slowly on a phone, the person who built it is gone, and nobody knows the login. That project is a rebuild, and it has its own rules about keeping the rankings you already have. We cover those on the [website redesign](/services/websites/redesign) page.
Both projects get the same foundation. The difference is where we start.

sections.heading: What a website has to do

blocks.text: If a site does not tell a stranger what the business does in one screen, it does not work, however good it looks. So the three jobs come in order.

blocks.title: Say what you do
blocks.text: What you do, who you do it for, where, and what happens next, on the first screen.

blocks.title: Design that says it
blocks.text: The layout has to carry that message, which is a different job from writing it.

blocks.title: Read well to machines
blocks.text: Google, and now the AI assistants people ask for recommendations, read the same page a customer does.
Most small business websites fail the first job. They open with a slogan, bury the phone number, and never say the city.

sections.heading: What small business website design includes

blocks.title: Copy first
blocks.text: We write it from a call with you, because the words decide the layout and not the other way round. The words are also what make the site yours; a template supplies everything except them.

blocks.title: Design, then a hand coded build
blocks.text: We hand code every site instead of using a drag and drop builder, which is why our pages pass Google's [Core Web Vitals](https://web.dev/articles/vitals) on a phone and why you keep full control of structure and speed later.

blocks.title: Search structure built in
blocks.text: Every site ships with one page per service, one keyword per page, proper titles and headings, schema markup, and plain question and answer sections that AI assistants can lift. For a local business, that last part is what gets you named when a customer asks ChatGPT instead of Google; the details are in [AEO for local businesses](/blog/aeo-for-local-businesses). Forms connect to your inbox or your [CRM](/services/crm) so a lead never sits unread. We hand over the domain, the code, and the CMS access, and we train you on the CMS before we leave.

sections.heading: Built for what the site has to do

blocks.text: A service business needs a page for each service, because that is how people search and how Google ranks. A one offer business needs a landing page that does one thing well. A studio needs a portfolio that loads 40 images without stalling. A clinic needs booking.
We ask what the site is for before we open a design tool. Sometimes the answer is a three page site and a strong Google Business Profile, and that is the proposal you get.

sections.heading: Websites that get found

blocks.text: Structure is what brings the visitor. Design is what keeps them.

We proved the first half on our own domain: a blank site went to 204 ranked keywords, 265K impressions, and 39 AI citations in 6 months with no ad spend. The whole thing is in the [organic growth case study](/work/rsla-organic-growth). When we rebuilt [Fieldshare](/work/fieldshare-seo-website-rebrand), a field management platform for oil and gas operators, the new site went on to be cited by ChatGPT, Gemini, and Google AI for their core topics.
If you want us to keep working on rankings after launch, that is a separate service, [SEO services](/services/seo), and the site is built to support it either way.

faqHeading: Questions people ask before hiring us

faqs.q: How much does small business website design cost?
faqs.a: One fixed price for the whole project, quoted after one call, and it does not move once you sign. What moves the number is the page count, whether the site needs booking, online ordering, or custom functionality, and how much existing content has to be migrated. A 5 page site for a plumber and a 40 page site with a store are different projects, and the proposal says which one you need.

faqs.q: How long does it take to build a website?
faqs.a: 4 to 6 weeks from kickoff to launch for most projects. A focused single page site can ship faster. A larger site with custom functionality can take up to 8 weeks. The timeline is in the proposal before we start.

faqs.q: Do I own my website?
faqs.a: Yes. Domain, code, content, and CMS access are all yours the day the project closes. There is no vendor lock in and no monthly fee to keep what you paid for.

faqs.q: Can I just build it myself with Wix or an AI builder?
faqs.a: You can, and it may look fine. The problem is not the look. Template builders share layouts across hundreds of businesses, limit your control over speed and structure, and the AI builders skip the keyword plan, the page structure, and the content that gets a site found. For some stages a builder is the right call, and then the first call ends there, with no proposal.
